title: Google Launches LiteRT Tensor API for Building, Customizing, and Optimizing ML Models for On-Device
gist: Google released the LiteRT Tensor API, a C++ API for authoring ML model graphs that run across CPU, GPU and NPU, with a SAM 2 demo built by a coding agent running about 1.5x faster than Apple MLX on a MacBook Pro. An Arm AI director advises starting with model conversion and using the C++ API only when graph-level control is needed.

insights.claim: Google introduced the LiteRT Tensor API, a lightweight C++ API for building, customizing and optimizing machine learning models directly for on-device execution, combining native model authoring flexibility with cross-platform portability.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Google is pushing on-device ML tooling toward portable, hardware-agnostic authoring, relevant to edge-AI platform competition.
insights.quote: Google has introduced the LiteRT Tensor API, a lightweight C++ API

insights.claim: The traditional approach of hand-writing C++ computations ties implementations to specific backends such as Metal, OpenCL or Vulkan, forcing rewrites for each new hardware target and heavy manual work on zero-copy buffers and CPU/GPU/NPU synchronization.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Backend fragmentation is the cost the API targets; abstraction layers that remove it capture developer lock-in.

insights.claim: The API lets developers build computation graphs operation by operation in C++ and run the same graphs through LiteRT on CPU, GPU and NPU without per-target rewrites.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Write-once accelerator portability lowers the cost of supporting new silicon, including NPUs.
insights.locator: The LiteRT Tensor API aims to address

insights.claim: Other key features are direct weight loading from checkpoints including Hugging Face .safetensors files, zero-copy buffer interoperability across pre-processing, inference and post-processing, and compatibility with AI coding agents that generate C++ to construct, modify, validate and benchmark graphs.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Direct ingestion of the dominant open-weights format ties Google's on-device stack into the Hugging Face ecosystem.

insights.claim: Google ran the same C++ SAM 2 code on the GPUs of a macOS laptop (Metal), an iOS phone (Metal) and an Android phone (OpenCL), and reports about 1.5x faster than Apple MLX on a MacBook Pro (fp16, image encoder plus mask decoder).
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: A vendor-reported claim that Google's cross-platform stack can beat Apple's native framework on Apple hardware; self-reported and not independently verified.
insights.quote: In our tests on the MacBook Pro, it ran about 1.5x faster than Apple MLX

insights.claim: Because the model graph is defined in plain C++, a coding agent could optimize it, for example moving SAM 2's per-frame visibility decisions from CPU code into the graph and rewriting operations that caused CPU fallback on WebGPU.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Structured, code-defined graphs make ML performance tuning a task agents can automate, which compresses optimization labor.

insights.claim: Arm's Laurence Moroney cites a coding-agent-driven improvement from under 10 to over 30 frames per second at 512x512 on WebGPU as evidence that structured primitives help agents do real optimization work.
insights.speaker: Laurence Moroney
insights.so_what: A 3x speedup attributed to agent iteration is anecdotal but supports the thesis that agents improve hardware-level ML code.
insights.quote: Going from under 10 to over 30 frames per second at 512x512 on WebGPU

insights.claim: Moroney advises developers to start with model conversion and turn to the C++ API only when they need graph-level control or want pre- and post-processing to stay on the accelerator.
insights.speaker: Laurence Moroney
insights.so_what: Signals the Tensor API is an advanced tool, not the default path, which limits near-term adoption breadth.
insights.quote: when you need graph-level control or want pre and post-processing to stay on the accelerator

insights.claim: Google's planned improvements include direct ML Drift backend support, additional NPU-friendly operations, automatic full-graph quantization, and expanded dynamic-shape support for varying image sizes, batch sizes and sequence lengths.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: NPU-friendly ops and automatic quantization point to Google prioritizing on-device accelerator utilization.
